items.title: 6th Annual Symposium on Pop Culture and International Law: Genocide in the Canvas? International Law and the Destruction of Lumière in Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
items.summary: [Dr Laurence Atkin-Teillet is a Lecturer in International Criminal and Humanitarian Law at Nottingham Law School, Nottingham Trent University.] What makes a world real? Is it the material from whic…
items.content:
[ Dr Laurence Atkin-Teillet is a Lecturer in International Criminal and Humanitarian Law at Nottingham Law School, Nottingham Trent University.]

What makes a world real? Is it the material from which it is made, the person who created it, or the lives of those who inhabit it? And if a world contains beings who think, love, suffer, build communities and fear their own destruction, does it matter that they were painted into existence rather than born?

These questions are at the heart of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , the role-playing game developed by Sandfall Interactive . They also raise a very difficult question for international law: could the deliberate destruction of an entire population of human-like beings constitute genocide, even if those beings exist inside a painting?

The answer under existing international law is obviously not straightforward. Yet the question does show some important assumptions about the groups whom international law protects, the nature of personhood, and the boundaries between what we consider real and what we consider worthy of legal protection.

At first, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 appears to tell a story of a population living under the shadow of an existential threat. Its inhabitants live in Lumière, a city in a strange and beautiful world shaped by magic.

Each year, a figure known as the Paintress marks a new number on a distant Monolith. This number determines the age of those who will disappear in an event known as the Gommage . When the number changes to 33, everyone aged 33 vanishes, leaving families and friends to mourn those they have lost. Expedition 33 sets out to stop the Paintress and end the cycle. As the story continues, however, the distinction between reality and fiction begins to disappear.

The Canvas is not an imaginary world inhabited by characters who exist for the entertainment of an audience – it is a world created through the artistic powers of the Dessendre family. The real-world painter Verso created the Canvas; following his death, his mother, Aline, retreated into it and recreated aspects of the family she had lost. The world came to contain painted versions of people, alongside other beings with their own lives and identities.

Aline’s husband, Renoir, enters the Canvas in an attempt to bring her back to reality. Their conflict gradually threatens the survival of the world and its inhabitants. The struggle becomes even more complicated when we discover that Maelle is the real-world Alicia, who entered the Canvas and lost her former identity, while the painted Verso is a recreation of the real Verso.

The game’s ending presents a difficult choice. In Verso’s ending, often nicknamed the “ Genocide Ending ”, he defeats Maelle and destroys the Canvas. The painted world and the inhabitants whom the player has come to know disappear. In Maelle’s ending, she preserves the Canvas, but her decision also raises questions about autonomy and the right to determine one’s own existence.

The choice is between two understandings of what makes a life worth preserving. The painted inhabitants may have been created by another person, but they experience relationships, loss, fear and attachment – their lives have meaning to them. From their perspective, the destruction of the Canvas is the end of their world.

And that’s why I started wondering: could destroying the Canvas and everyone who lives in it amount to genocide?

Article II of the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide defines genocide through two central requirements: certain prohibited acts must be committed with the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such. The prohibited acts include killing members of the group, causing them serious bodily or mental harm, deliberately inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about their physical destruction, imposing measures intended to prevent births, and forcibly transferring children to another group.

The definition is reproduced in Article 6 of the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court .

Can the Inhabitants of Lumière Constitute an Ethnic Group?

items.title: Mass Effect Could Still Be Saved, Ex-BioWare Developer Suggests, With Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Holding the Key
items.summary: The future of Mass Effect could be secured with a key learning from the beloved Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, a former BioWare veteran has suggested.
items.content:
The future of Mass Effect could be secured with a key learning from the beloved Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, a former BioWare veteran has suggested.

In the days since EA announced it was shutting down its storied RPG game studio and killing its in-development Mass Effect Universe project, discussion has turned to the costs behind creating another AAA-budget entry in BioWare's space opera series, following a report that EA decided to invest in Star Wars instead .

Last week, BioWare co-founder Trent Oster suggested that EA would likely have been on the hook for at least $200 million in development costs to finish Mass Effect Universe at a level that fans expected.

"Rough ballpark (based on contemporaries) is $200m+," Oster wrote on X/Twitter. "That is a big number to commit up front. There has to be a bigger plan in place for the IP to make the math work." (To be fair, there is still that Mass Effect TV series in the works. And there certainly won't be any bigger plan in place for the IP if its flagship next game is cancelled.)

Now, Mass Effect lead programmer Christina Norman has said the game could be made for around $50 million — a figure that is five times the budget spent by the makers of Clair Obscur.

Highlighting a report on the French-made RPG's overall budget, which was pegged at less than $10 million, Norman wrote on X/Twitter that this was "a good example of why I think another Mass Effect game could be made for well under 200 million.

"I mean 5x the budget of Claire obscure expedition 33 should be more than enough," she continued. "You can always spend more but clever small teams can get it done."

Norman spent more than six years at BioWare working on the original Mass Effect trilogy, firstly as a lead programmer responsible for creating the franchise's conversation system, before moving on to become lead designer for Mass Effect 2 and 3, working to improve the series' gameplay.

In the years since, Norman served stints at Riot Games and her own co-founded startup, before becoming a full-time machine learning engineering consultant focused on LLM-directed character conversations. Still, there's no suggestion that LLM technology would be needed to turn in Mass Effect Universe on a smaller budget.

Even Oster has said he believed a new Mass Effect could be made for "cheaper" than $200m, though it "wouldn’t be what the team described in the Universe concept," he wrote in a follow-up post. Alas, Oster also highlighted another big blocker to a new Mass Effect being made — that EA still owns the franchise's rights, and may never want to give them up, even if it's not actively using them. "The big push would be getting the IP free," he concluded. "The fans deserve more."

Last week's annual N7 Day celebration of the Mass Effect franchise featured the Normandy's cast and crew teaming up for a video message asking fans to help save Mass Effect . This followed an array of footage and details for the canceled Mass Effect Universe appearing online, and a petition for EA to reconsider its decision which has gained more than 325,000 signatures . A Canadian politician also started a government petition to save BioWare just last week.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

items.title: Big Walk Studio Explains Undisclosed AI Use Following Indie GOTY Disqualification
items.summary: It has emerged after an independent awards body discounted it from GOTY contention.
items.content:
Big Walk Studio Explains Undisclosed AI Use Following Indie GOTY Disqualification From TheGamer (Written by Josh Coulson) on November 10, 2026 | OpenCritic

AI use in video games has never been a more hotly debated topic, and much like last year with Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , its masked use during development has impacted one of this year’s Game of the Year frontrunners, Big Walk . Turns out AI was used during Big Walk’s development, and it’s the game’s disqualification from the Independent Game Festival’s GOTY consideration that has led to that unfortunate discovery.

The IGF posted a statement (thanks, Aftermath ) regarding its nominations this year, highlighting that some who vote for its GOTY nominees and award winners simply won’t consider games that used generative AI during their development. It seemed a fairly straightforward, somewhat expected stance. However, it became clear in the hours after that statement was posted that the reason IGF representatives were having such a tough time deliberating is because AI was used during Big Walk’s development.

As the BDS Boycott continues, Big Walk stands firm.

That revelation has led to Big Walk studio House House updating its FAQ to confirm that yes, AI was used during the game’s development process, and to explain how exactly it was implemented.

items.title: Game Awards 2026: All Game of the Year Front-Runners and Predictions
items.content:
By Oli Welsh Updated Nov 9, 2026, 4:51 PM EST GOTY Watch What’s in pole position for gaming’s top prize? Let’s make some predictions

Image: Nintendo EPD/Nintendo Add Polygon.com on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover Sign in to your Polygon.com account Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread 59 Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap With only a month to go until the 13th Game Awards, set for Dec. 10, every key competitor but one (the big one) has been released. The likelihood of anything emerging to stop Grand Theft Auto 6 from sweeping the night looks increasingly slim in what is turning out to be a much weaker year than it looked on paper.

At this point, we have a clear idea of what games will be favored by The Game Awards' voting body : A high Metacritic rating (preferably over 90) is a must; role-playing games and action-adventures are strongly favored, as are games with strong narrative elements; indie and multiplayer games struggle harder for recognition than AAA single-player adventures. We used these metrics to correctly predict last year's winner, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , and the 2024 winner, Astro Bot . In 2025, we also predicted all six GOTY nominees and correctly called 20 other categories.

Below, you'll find our predictions for the most likely nominees, of which there are six each year, for Game of the Year 2026 — taken only from games that have already been released (or made available for review). We'll update these rankings throughout the year as new games are released. We'll also list some likely upcoming contenders and some of the 2026 GOTY race's dark horses, too.

Update (Nov. 9): The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has emerged as the highest-rated game of the year to date, and critical acclaim has been followed by a huge wave of social love as players share their rediscovery of the classic adventure. Ocarina 's status as a dead-cert for a GOTY nomination is only matched by the seeming impossibility of a remake of a 28-year-old game winning Game of the Year. That said, it looks stronger than much of the competition, most of which is struggling to maintain momentum in one way or another; the most recent entry, Phantom Blade Zero, seems to have failed to capture the conversation.

Resident Evil Requiem screenshot Image: Capcom Why it could win: Resident Evil is a reliable contender at The Game Awards , with three GOTY nominations since 2019, and many more in other categories. Requiem combines the fan appeal of the remakes with the freshness of a new entry, and blends their gameplay successfully, too. It's slickly produced, digestible, thrilling, with both global appeal and a serious side: a perfect Game Awards GOTY contender.

Weaknesses: Requiem 's critical reception was very good overall, but perhaps a tiny bit soft to be a true GOTY contender — it sits in the high 80s on Metacritic and OpenCritic. How well it fares in the long run will depend on the strength of the competition, but for now, it's in the lead.

Momentum (holding steady): Potential challengers to Requiem 's status as pack leader just keep falling by the wayside. Nothing else released this year combines critical acclaim with a perfect Game Awards genre profile so effectively, and nothing else will until GTA 6 comes out. It's a lock for a nomination.

Read Giovanni Colantonio's full review of Resident Evil Requiem .

Image: Nintendo EPD/Nintendo Why it could win: A beloved classic, with a reputation as the best game ever made, lavishly remade by a team at the top of their game, and showered in critical plaudits like no other game this year. It may be just a remake, but Nintendo has mustered a huge sense of event around Ocarina , from its dramatic visual reinvention to its bold positioning against GTA 6 in the calendar.

Weaknesses: After all, though, it's still a remake of an old game, and a very faithful one. The jury will want to recognize Nintendo's achievement here (as it has done for the likes of Resident Evil 4 and Final Fantasy 7 Remake in the past), but a Game of the Year win seems inconceivable for such a well known quantity.

Momentum (new entry): Shortly after launch, Ocarina fever is at an all-time high and shows little sign of abating. And while the art direction initially seemed divisive, players and press alike seem united in their praise.

Read Giovanni Colantonio's full review of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time .

Image: House House/Panic Why it could win: House House's co-op puzzle adventure has a fantastic critical reputation — it currently sits at 91 on Metacritic, higher than any other game on this list. The developer has pedigree: Untitled Goose Game was a dark horse GOTY contender in 2019, and even won the overall award at DICE. It's a refined design in a currently voguish genre. Co-op games go down well at The Game Awards ( It Takes Two won in 2021). And there's a good chance jury members have had a good time playing it together.

items.title: The Ocarina of Time remake dethrones Expedition 33 as the highest-rated game by users
items.summary: It was bound to happen sooner or later. Up until now, the excellent Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 held the top spot in terms of player ratings with an impressive…
items.content:
It was bound to happen sooner or later. Up until now, the excellent Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 held the top spot in terms of player ratings with an impressive 9.4/10.

Now, the top spot on the podium belongs to The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2, which currently holds a score of 9.6/10 based on 2,100 reviews, which is truly exceptional.

Everyone is free to interpret this development as they see fit: should a remake be considered on par with an original title, especially when it comes from a new franchise and a new studio?

While at first glance this question may seem secondary given the unofficial nature of this highest player rating award, it could very well become much more relevant by the end of the year, with events like the Game Awards .

items.title: Game Pass Is About To Lose Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 And Some Other Incredible Games
items.summary: The RPG sensation and more gems are leaving in October
items.content:
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 was one of 2025’s best games and one of the best third-party releases ever to join Game Pass day-and-date. Players have now had over a year to finish the turn-based RPG, but for any subscribers who haven’t yet taken the plunge, time is running out. The GOTY winner is leaving Game Pass on October 15.

That leaves you just under two weeks to go and complete the journey or start it from scratch. You can rush the main story to clear it in under 30 hours, but if you want to mine all of the expanded content, a completionist run will take you more than twice that. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is one of the rare JRPG-inspired games that’s managed to break through in the modern era to a broader audience, in part thanks to its novel dodge and parry mechanics which inject some fresh energy into the usual turn-based grind. It’s also worth making it all the way through to hit the twist ending .

But Clair Obscur is also not the only great game leaving Game Pass this month . The full list includes:

Pacific Drive and A Plague Tale Requiem are both excellent, especially for the spooky month. The former is a sci-fi survival crafting game about navigating a zone full of strange anomalies with a haunted station wagon. The latter is about surviving a late medieval Europe infested with disease carrying rats. Donut County , on the other hand, is a light hearted puzzle game you can finish in just a few hours that is still one of my favorite indie games of all time.

items.content:
Expeditioners!

Following the huge demand from so many of you, we’ve been working super hard to be able to finally announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, is now available with Arabic text!

This brings the total number of supported languages to 20!

With the new Arabic language support, we had to consider additional changes to the game’s UI to ensure a smooth and enjoyable experience for Arabic-speaking players around the world.

Adding Arabic localization has been a true team effort over many months, from the incredible adaptation and localization work carried out by the linguists, to reworking the vast majority of the user interface for right-to-left reading, all the way through localization testing.

Every team involved brought passion and dedication to making this possible, and we couldn’t be more grateful for their work. We hope this update makes the story feel even more personal to our players.

Today’s update also includes some additional fixes and improvements. Read the full patch notes here!

Thank you all so much for your continued support! <3

Tomorrow comes.

~ The Expedition 33 Team

Today marks 1 year since we released Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. This past year has been an incredible journey and so we have a few things to share with you today. 

 

To celebrate the occasion, the team put together a special piece of artwork that we hope you will enjoy!

We're so thrilled, and honestly still quite overwhelmed, to announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 has officially reached 8 million copies sold!

Thank you so so much to every single person who has played, created art, shared, streamed, discussed, and supported this game!!

We've pushed a fun little update live today: new haircuts are now available in-game, giving the expedition even more style to strut around in! 💅 

For the full list of changes, fixes, and improvements, you can read the patch notes here

Our community is packed with phenomenally talented artists and we wanted to celebrate that today.  

We commissioned some of our amazing community creators to design official Expedition 33 emotes for you to use in your own channels! 

A massive thank you to IrunoArt, comickergirl (Sarah Leuver), and Bugyakis for their brilliant work on each of these!!

They're FREE to download and use here

It's been a big day for us. Thank you for making it possible. 🎂 

And if you know someone who wants to pick up the game, we're running a 20% sale right now on Steam - As well as some fun merchandise goodies available on our merch page!

Merch Page

From the bottom of our hearts, we’re so thankful to each and every one of you – this has been the best year of our lives, thanks to you. 

 

- The Expedition 33 Team

items.content:
Introducing a special bundle featuring the award‑winning fantasy RPG “Metaphor: ReFantazio”, created by the team behind Persona 3-5, paired with “Clair Obscur: Expedition 33” - now available at 10% off!

Enjoy both titles and experience the worlds for yourself!

The Metaphor: ReFantazio × Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Bundle includes two games: “Metaphor: ReFantazio” and “Clair Obscur: Expedition 33.”

Message from Guillaume Broche & Katsura Hashino

"Metaphor: ReFantazio is a game that is really inspiring for us. It tells a beautiful story in a completely new world that is masterfully crafted. It deals with heavy themes but one that resonates strongly with me is the importance of imagination in all aspects of our lives. The cast is lovable and the turn-based battle system is one of the best I have played. The re-imagination of the traditional jobs system through Archetypes is fantastic and opens up so many playstyles that are fun to play around with. On top of that, the game has one of the most charismatic villains I've ever seen in an RPG. It is a great honor to be able to collaborate with Atlus on this bundle, as I have been a fan of their work since Shin Megami Tensei: Lucifer's Call (also known as Shin Megami Tensei III Nocturne for some players)." - Guillaume Broche

"I am Katsura Hashino from ATLUS, serving as the Creative Director for “Metaphor: ReFantazio.” I am very pleased to hear that a Steam bundle will be released with “Expedition 33,” a title that has received high praise around the world.

“Expedition 33” is a work that conveys a deep understanding of and sincere dedication to the JRPG genre, crafted with great care down to the finest details. As someone who also creates RPGs, I found it to be truly inspiring.

I am genuinely delighted to see Japanese-style RPGs being born and embraced, not only from Japanese-based studios like ours, but other places around the world through diverse creative approaches.

While the two titles differ in their worlds and overall direction, players may find a shared spirit in how we each approach and express the RPG genre. I hope that this bundle encourages players to experience both titles and enjoy the breadth of what RPGs can offer."

items.summary: Expeditioners, We're so pleased to see so many of you enjoying the new photo mode feature!! We put a lot of time and care into building this feature and we’re so glad to see so many of you enjoying it! There were a lot of moving parts invol
items.content:
Expeditioners,

We're so pleased to see so many of you enjoying the new photo mode feature!!

We put a lot of time and care into building this feature and we’re so glad to see so many of you enjoying it! There were a lot of moving parts involved in getting the Photo Mode set up, so we thought we’d show a bit of the process in this blog and talk a bit about what went into building this feature.

There were a few key people involved in the development of this, and each of them had a part to write here !

VINCENT CONSTANTIN-TURKI – Producer \

One of the main features we wanted to introduce with the Thank You Update was Photo Mode. It felt like a meaningful way to give something back to the players and thank them for their commitment to the game.

What’s funny is that the team in charge of developing Photo Mode doesn’t usually use this feature in other games, which is why we decided to collaborate with Shinobi. He helped us design a Photo Mode that would truly resonate with players.

NAJA DALMAGNE – QA Coordinator \

In many games we tested, Photo Modes often felt restrictive, which could quickly become frustrating. So, from the very beginning, one of the key goals we all agreed on was to give players as much freedom as possible. It was really about letting players express their creativity without getting in the way.

During development, the QA team ran into some unexpected and sometimes quite funny issues. One of the funniest, but also one of the most severe, involved characters whose heads or torsos could become displaced or deformed when opening the Photo Mode if they hadn’t been visible on screen for a while during exploration.

One feature I’m particularly proud of is the lighting system Florian worked on. It offers great flexibility while remaining fairly easy to use, which really makes a difference when you're trying to get the perfect shot.

FLORIAN TORRES – Senior Gameplay Programmer \ \

I love giving players as many tools and features as possible (that’s literally the purpose of my job).

When we started working on the photo mode, our goal was to give players as few restrictions as possible and that’s what I was in charge of coding: infinite camera distance, the ability to pass through collisions, lots of customizable lights, many (weird) filters, and more.

Of course, that comes with its challenges, but in the end it allows players to see a lot of things we don’t want to show during normal gameplay. The photo mode became a way to peek behind the scenes of each cinematic or environment, and sometimes even see how we have created the entire game.

Ever wondered what happens outside the camera frame? Here’s an example (sorry cinematic team, I love you).

LUDOVIC ‘SHINOBI’ HELME – Photo Mode Consultant \

We felt it was important to include anything that increases the “freedom” factor for players. It opens up countless possibilities every time someone enters photo mode: a very generous camera range to capture unseen details or create epic compositions, RGB curves control to edit and build your own color schemes, a strong custom lighting system to truly take ownership of a scene, and solid depth-of-field management.

But when all of that is also available in cutscenes - giving access to those incredible facial expressions and emotions - that’s when I really start to feel satisfied.

Every shot I’ve seen has blown my mind, and I often wish I’d been the one to come up with the idea. It’s truly inspiring.

I’m very proud that the team managed to create a tool that is both beginner-friendly and deeply satisfying for more experienced photographers. Finding that balance is extremely difficult.

With all of these features, there had to be a user-friendly way for people to make use of everything. Making sure players had full control of all the settings and could navigate all the features comes down to our awesome Gameplay & UI Programmer, VICTOR BOULEZ.

Thank you for all of your appreciation and feedback on this feature, we had a lot of fun making it and even more fun watching you use it!

This past week, especially, we’ve really loved the work you’ve all been putting into the social Photo Mode Prompt Challenge!! We’ve seen some amazing photography this past week, it’s completely blown our minds how creative you have been able to get with the prompts and tools.

Even though the challenge is over, feel free to keep sharing your work with us on social media, we thoroughly enjoy seeing some of your masterpieces!!

In the meantime, we are continuing to work on fixes for ongoing problems, keep an eye on the bug thread and socials to stay updated on the latest.

Finally, we leave you with some of our favourite uses of photo mode.

items.title: How ‘Clair Obscur: Expedition 33’ Revitalized the RPG and Won Game of the Year
items.summary: A French turn-based RPG made for under $10 million somehow managed to be the defining game of 2025. Now, Hollywood is calling.
items.content:
This year, gamers beheld the strangest of success stories: (1) A French video game publisher (2) that isn’t Ubisoft (3) partnered with a rookie studio (4) that is also French (5) to release a turn-based role-playing game (6) with a decidedly Parisian flamboyance (7) that would commercially outperform every other single-player title out this year by a mile.

The game was Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 . Its developer, Sandfall Interactive, and its publisher, Kepler Interactive, were hardly household names upon the game’s release in April 2025; both companies were founded in just the past couple of years, during COVID, and while Kepler already had one hit to its credit in Sifu , Clair Obscur was, in fact, the debut title for Sandfall Interactive. This was a less than $10 million project in a world of $200 million franchise titles. Yet Clair Obscur was a blockbuster in scope and a marvel in several aspects of its execution—in its wonderfully tense combat, in its immense musical score, in its gorgeous art direction, in its remarkably mature writing. It was shockingly on par with Final Fantasy . It was, in fact, something bigger.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 sold 1 million copies in three days and more than 6 million copies by the end of the year. It’s become the year’s defining video game release, and it’s slated to become a full franchise, from a studio that is only getting started. The Hollywood production company Story Kitchen, which specializes in video game adaptations, is already handling a live-action film adaptation of Clair Obscur . Earlier this month, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, publicly congratulated Sandfall after Clair Obscur swept the Game Awards in Los Angeles, beating Death Stranding 2 and Hollow Knight: Silksong for Game of the Year.

Beginning in the dreamy island town of Lumière—conspicuously evocative of Paris circa the Belle Époque— Clair Obscur is the story of a defiant humanity staring down the threat of extinction.

Lumière is haunted by a distant figure known as the Paintress, who oversees an ominous countdown that’s displayed on the face of a monolith that looms over the horizon. The countdown drops by one each year, and the number represents an age: Anyone at or over the age that’s currently displayed is erased from existence, in an annual phenomenon known as the gommage. These heartless erasures leave the survivors ever more desperate to vanquish the Paintress. The beleaguered people of Lumière send waves of armed expeditions to the monolith across the sea. The dozens of expeditions to date have all failed, littering the landscape with withered corpses, ruined campsites, and scattered logs of each team’s discoveries in the treacherous world beyond Lumière.

A young soldier named Gustave leads Expedition 33, the latest, fateful voyage to defeat the Paintress. So we follow Gustave, Maelle, Lune, Sciel, and a few other stragglers through a series of uncomfortable subversions of the genre’s standard sentimental journey to save the world. In so many ways, Clair Obscur ends in a place very different from where it began, after a series of profound revelations and existential reckonings straight from Sartre and Descartes. The game’s director, Guillaume Broche, thus pitched Clair Obscur to its composer, Lorien Testard: “You arrive at the beginning of the game after the heroes have already lost.”

Chiefly, Clair Obscur tends to draw comparisons to Final Fantasy X , a game that’s similarly concerned with a world-saving pilgrimage that was secretly doomed from the very start. The comparison is still more striking at the historical level: FFX is widely seen as both the technical and commercial peak of the triple-A turn-based RPG, preceding a couple of decades of agonizing among some players about the inventiveness and the fashionability of these sorts of games.

RPG Party: ‘Clair Obscur: Expedition 33’ and ‘The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Remastered’

svg]:ui-size-4 p-0 ui-bg-transparent ui-text-brand-orange ui-flex md:ui-hidden" data-sentry-component="MediumIcon" data-sentry-source-file="index.tsx"> Button Mash Button Mash On the one hand, games like Persona 5 , Octopath Traveler , Metaphor: ReFantazio , and now Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 are some of the bestselling single-player titles of the past decade, and they’re all turn-based RPGs. Still, the heyday of the turn-based RPG was squarely in the late ’90s through the early 2000s, with their popularity having since waned in favor of real-time, action-based RPGs such as Elden Ring . Square Enix, the longtime publisher of Final Fantasy , has for the past several years struggled to adapt its banner franchise to these shifting sensibilities; Final Fantasy XV and the most recent Final Fantasy XVI both implemented purely action-based combat systems, to the widespread displeasure of many longtime fans of the series. (The ongoing remake trilogy for Final Fantasy VII , a turn-based classic, uses a peculiar hybrid system for its combat: free, real-time movement with turn-based actions.)

Sandfall opted to integrate real-time prompts into the turn-based combat of Clair Obscur . Here, the player selects a move for a character in battle—a basic attack, a healing spell, a party buff, etc.—and then executes quick time inputs during the move’s animation in order to increase its effectiveness. More importantly, Clair Obscur lets players respond to incoming attacks by dodging, parrying, or jumping, depending on the type of attack. These defensive options, varying in execution difficulty, give the player opportunities to avoid taking any damage from a hit, with a successful parry of an entire combo also unleashing an instant counterattack. So here we have a system of turn-based combat that tests a player’s real-time reflexes, akin to a rhythm game, rewarding a mix of savviness in weapon selection, stat management, and party composition, as in classic turn-based RPGs.

Clair Obscur feels like a distinct breakthrough, though not for a lack of creative effort by the industry in previous years to reinvent the turn-based RPG. The cult classic Lost Odyssey , for instance, experimented with timed, reflex-based elements in turn-based combat to divisive effect in the era of its release. This is the typical conundrum for developers hoping to reinvigorate or revolutionize the turn-based RPG: how to improve upon the old mechanics rather than distort them in the hands of their most loyal fan bases. Broche has cited Lost Odyssey as a major influence in the development of Clair Obscur . He approached his game’s release date with a certain mischievous daring, a willingness to treat experimental features as unquestionably ready—no, destined—for prime time.

items.title: We're finalists in the Steam Awards!!
items.summary: Expeditioners, As we get closer to the holidays and towards the end of 2025, looking back on the year we cannot fathom everything that we've been gifted by you all. Thank you all so so much for nominating Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 as a fi
items.content:
Expeditioners,

As we get closer to the holidays and towards the end of 2025, looking back on the year we cannot fathom everything that we've been gifted by you all.

Thank you all so so much for nominating Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 as a finalist in Steam's Game of the Year and Best Soundtrack awards!! We could not be more grateful for your ongoing support ❤️❤️

Please do take a look at all the other amazing nominees and finalists in this year's event - we have completely loved so many games this year and are so honoured to be among them!!

Thank you for making 2025 such a MAGICAL year for all of us. Wishing you all the happiest of holidays and a wonderful new year!!!

Tomorrow comes.

~ The Expedition 33 Team
